lines.note: This Taqe means another house or family, glossed by Tano iye. The initial capital T is abraded; its residual upper stroke and same-page capital comparators support the incorporated reading.
This separate Taqe concerns stature or bodily height. A pilcrow introduces an example divided Ta- / qeno across physical lines.
The initial fragment completes Taqeno in the example of a tall person. It closes the stature entry, not the separate bamboo headword below.
This Taqe denotes bamboo. It is a complete one-line homograph and remains separate from the following mountain-summit sense.

runs.text: Alto, ou cume da ſerra, ou monte: a

lines.note: This homograph denotes the top or summit of a mountain or ridge. The source adds a qualification about the proper word on the next line.
The dictionary says the proper word is Daqe. That Japanese term is visibly italic inside the Portuguese explanation; it is recorded in typeface_terms without silently changing the scan's typeface.
The verb Taqe is introduced with its inflected forms and a sense of rising high. Vt announces the first example on the following line.
Figa taqeta means that the sun is high. A new example begins Faru, referring to spring, and continues with summer on the next line.
The expression describes spring or summer advancing toward its end. The Portuguese seasonal name is divided prima ve- / ra across physical lines.
The seasonal example finishes with spring and summer. A new example, Chiyeno taqeta fito, concerns a person of advanced knowledge rather than physical height.
The alternative taqeta fito shares the sense of a person with great knowledge. This completes the knowledge-related example within the verb's extended meanings.
This example describes a courageous person. Qimono here belongs to the expression involving spirit or courage, not the clothing word; eſfor- continues below.
The first fragment completes eſforçado. A new example concerns a highly learned person, with its Portuguese translation divided Grã- / de.
The learned-person example ends. Toxiga taqeta fito introduces an older person, and Ho- begins the Portuguese Homem continued below.

runs.text: mem ja de muita idade como de quarenta por

lines.note: The source describes someone already of considerable age, giving forty onward as an example. This historical age characterization is transcribed, not adopted as a modern judgment.
Diante completes the phrase meaning from forty onward. It closes the age example and the extended verbal entry Taqe.

runs.text: Faxis de cana com que ſe come.

lines.note: Taqebaxi denotes cane or bamboo chopsticks used for eating. The source reads baxi, and its Portuguese explanation is complete on this line.
Taqebaxira denotes bamboo columns or pillars. The plural Colunnas is retained as printed rather than reduced to a singular form.
Taqebayaxi denotes a bamboo grove or stand of canes. The two Portuguese equivalents form a complete one-line definition.

runs.text: Murrão feito de caſca de bambus.

lines.note: Taqebinaua denotes a matchcord made from bamboo bark. The narrow i after b is damaged; reinspection after the supplied NINJAL index comparison supports binaua, correcting an earlier tentative banaua reading. Reference attribution: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The reference was consulted after independent scan reading, not imported as normalized canonical text.

runs.text: O igualar ſe pera ver quẽ he mais

lines.note: Taqecurabe first means standing together or comparing to see who is taller. The Portuguese explanation continues on the next line.

runs.text: alto do corpo. ¶ Itẽ, permet. Fazer pro-

lines.note: The height-comparison sense ends. A metaphorical extension introduces testing or comparing other qualities, with pro- continuing as ua below.

runs.text: ua, ou comparação das forças, habilidade, le-

lines.note: The comparison extends to strength, ability, and learning. The visible i in habilidade is retained, and le- begins letras on the next line.
Tras completes letras, learning or scholarship. Taqecurabeuo ſuru supplies the verbal example for making these comparisons.
Taqedaruqi denotes a bamboo roof timber or rafter. The source's historical Portuguese Aguieiro is retained rather than replaced by a modern construction term.
Taqefubaco is a tube for holding letters. The definition is complete on this physical line, with no additional material or construction details supplied.
Taqegaqi denotes a bamboo hedge or fence. This compact entry is complete and remains separate from the recreational activity on the following line.

runs.text: Certo folguedo de ir a õde ha canas.

lines.note: Taqegari is described as a recreation involving going where canes grow. The nasal abbreviation in õde is retained, without adding details not stated in the definition.
Taqegatana, alternatively fadaqegatana, denotes a currycomb. The Portuguese description of its use and shape continues on the following two lines.

runs.text: dos caualos feita de cana à maneira de Cata-

lines.note: The currycomb is for horses and is made from cane in a swordlike shape. Cata- continues as na on the next line.
The line completes Catana and specifies teeth on the implement. This closes the bamboo currycomb entry and its shape comparison.
Taqegauara, also tacagauara, refers to bamboo used for roofing. The nasal ending in ſeruẽ is retained, and the purpose continues below.

runs.text: pera cubrir caſas em lugar de telha.

lines.note: The bamboo covers houses in place of roof tiles. This completes the roofing definition without converting the historical spelling cubrir to a modern form.
Taqei describes strength and fierceness, compared first to a brave soldier. The sequence of comparisons continues on the next physical line.
The comparison includes a spirited soldier or a fierce lion. The source's lião spelling is retained and completes the adjective's examples.
Taqen, glossed by Tani miſuru, means showing a thing to another person. The Portuguese ou- continues as tro below.
The first fragment completes outro. The prohibitive example reads arubecarazu, not arubecatazu, and its Portuguese translation begins an instruction not to show something.
This completes the instruction not to show the thing to anyone. It closes the example under Taqen.
Taqeno fada refers to the innermost thin layer of bamboo. The source's explanation of its medicinal use continues on the following line.

runs.text: do bambu que ſe toma pera mezinha.

lines.note: The inner bamboo layer is described as being taken medicinally. This historical use is transcribed without presenting it as a safe or effective modern treatment.

runs.text: Hũa fruita que dão os bambus co-

lines.note: Taqenomi is bamboo fruit or seed, compared with wheat seed. The source reads fruita, not frutia; co- continues as mo below.
This completes the comparison with wheat seed. The line closes Taqenomi without adding botanical detail beyond the printed explanation.
This noun Taqeri denotes a whale's penis. It is a separate lexical entry from the identically written verb for raging or roaring below.
The verb Taqeri gives its inflected forms, including etta, and describes extreme displays of anger. The physical actions continue on the following line.
The angry display involves shouting or roaring. A pilcrow introduces an example with a wild boar as subject, continuing below.
The example describes a wild boar rooting in the earth in its rage. The Portuguese mon- continues as tes on the next line.

runs.text: tes com o focinho aterra de braueza, & ſa-

lines.note: The boar roots the ground with its snout from ferocity and anger. The joined aterra is retained; ſa- continues as nha across the column boundary.
Nha completes ſanha from the left column. A new example concerns restraining a warrior eager for battle, with todo- continuing on the following line.
The Japanese example says that the restrained warrior rages because he wants to go forward. The Portuguese translation begins Im- and continues below.

runs.text: pedindo a hum fidalgo que eſtaua muito deſe-

lines.note: The translation describes preventing a noble warrior who was very eager to fight. The divided deſe- continues as joſo on the next line.

runs.text: joſo, & aluoraçado pera pelejar, fazia eſtremos

lines.note: The warrior is eager and excited for combat and responds with extreme displays. The description of his angry behaviour continues below.
The warrior fumes and roars in anger. This closes the extended Taqeri example that began in the left column.

runs.text: Repairos feitos de feixes de bãbus

lines.note: Taqetaba denotes defensive works made from bundles of bamboo. The nasal spelling bãbus is retained; the threats they protect against are stated below.
The bamboo defences protect against arrows and gunfire. This completes the historical description without adding construction or tactical instructions.
Taqetaca is described only as a kind of paper. No manufacturing method or more specific material identification is added to the canonical entry.
Taqeuara denotes a bamboo grove. The complete definition occupies this one physical line and remains separate from the toy-horse entry below.
Taqevma, also Chicuba, denotes a cane horse used as a toy. The headword's v is retained rather than misread as r; the users are specified below.
Children play with the cane horse. The historical spelling mininos is retained and closes the Taqevma definition.
Taqezauo, alternatively tacazauo, names a long bamboo pole. The following lines describe its use with a boat or for another purpose.

runs.text: que ſerue de vara da embarcação, ou de outra

lines.note: The long bamboo serves as a boat pole or another implement. The concluding word of the alternative follows on the next physical line.
Couſa completes the open-ended alternative use of the long bamboo pole. This short line closes the Taqezauo entry.
The scan clearly prints b in Taqebunoco, a bamboo lattice or slatted surface. The supplied NINJAL entry 241b06 notes intended Taqezunoco; the printed anomaly is retained rather than emended.
Taqezzuna denotes a mooring line or thick rope. The readings Amarra, corda, and the two long s letters in groſſa are retained.
The rope is made from bamboo, completing the material specification under Taqezzuna. This line is an indented continuation, not a separate entry.
Taqeyari denotes bamboo spears without iron tips. The source gives a compact descriptive definition, with no further construction detail.

runs.text: Lugar como precipicio donde cae algũa

lines.note: Taqi describes a precipice-like place from which a substantial stream of water falls. The verb reads cae, not cac, and the explanation continues below.
The water descends from the high place, completing the waterfall-related definition. The joined dagoa is retained as source spelling.

runs.text: Fazer fogo com lenha, ou pa-

lines.note: The verb Taqi means making a fire with wood or straw. The inflected forms and the division pa- / lha are retained.
Lha completes palha. Fiuo taqu illustrates making fire, and a pilcrow introduces Xiuouo taqu, whose salt-making explanation appears below.
Xiuouo taqu means making salt. Furouo taqu introduces heating a bath, with the Portuguese fo- continuing as go on the following line.

runs.text: go nos banhos, ou aquentar agoa dos banhos.

lines.note: The explanation concerns firing baths or heating their water. It completes the Furouo taqu example without starting another entry.
A visible pilcrow introduces Cǒuo taqu, burning incense or aromatic substances. The line was already indented in the input; only its missing printed pilcrow is restored.
Taqibi denotes a wood fire. This complete noun entry is separate from the following word for the firewood itself.
Taqigui denotes firewood. The headword and its single-word Portuguese definition form a complete physical line and a distinct entry.

runs.text: Soar a agoa q̃ cae dalgũlugar al-

lines.note: Taqinari describes the sound of falling or rushing water. The source reads Soar a agoa, and the closely joined dalgũlugar is retained rather than respaced.

runs.text: to, ou rochedo, ou que dà nalgum lugar baixo,

lines.note: The water falls from a height or rock, or strikes a lower place. To completes alto from the preceding line, and the definition continues below.

runs.text: ou pedras como rio que vai correndo. ¶

lines.note: The description includes water striking stones, as in a flowing river. A pilcrow begins a Japanese example divided Xema- / cura across physical lines.
Cura completes Xemacura. The period following it is retained as printed; the Japanese passage describes loud rushing water and continues on the next line.
The Japanese example ends, followed by the roman citation label Feiq. The italic Portuguese translation begins Fazendo and continues below; Feiq. is recorded as a citation typeface term.

runs.text: grande estrondo o rio que daua em hum baixo,

lines.note: The translation describes a river making a great noise where it strikes a low place. This is continuous Portuguese explanation of the cited Japanese passage.

runs.text: & a agoa que andaua como às voltas hia mui

lines.note: The water is described as swirling while moving very swiftly. The sentence continues below, and the printed accent in às is retained.
The final words describe the water as swift and forceful. Impetuoſa retains its t, completing the cited example under Taqinari.
Taqimono first means firewood. Item introduces a further sense of an aromatic substance or perfume, whose examples continue on the next line.
The source lists examples of perfumes and then begins a garment-related Japanese example, divided Yxǒ- / ni. The f in perfumes is retained rather than confused with long s.
Ni completes Yxǒni in the example of perfuming garments. The final verb reads tomuru with r; the Portuguese object continues below.
Veſtidos completes the explanation as perfuming clothes. This closes the aromatic-substance sense and the Taqimono entry.
Taqiǒ denotes another place or settlement. The marked final vowel and historical spelling pouoação are retained in this complete entry.
Taqiſute gives verbal forms and begins the meaning of setting firewood alight and leaving it. The final part of that action continues below.
The wood is left burning, completing the compound verb's definition. The attached spelling deixala is preserved rather than modernized.
Taqitate means beginning to light a fire or making it burn up. Its inflected forms are retained, and the Portuguese explanation continues below.

runs.text: fogo, ou fazelo arder em chamas.

lines.note: The alternative phrasing is making the fire burn in flames. This completes Taqitate without combining it with the following poetic noun.
Taqitçu is labelled poetic and equated with Taqi, water falling from a height. The introductory P. is visibly italic here; i, and the Japanese form remain roman.

runs.text: Lugar onde cae a agoa da ſerra,

lines.note: Taqitçubo denotes the place where water falling from a mountain lands. Its alternative precipice wording continues on the final body line.
This completes the definition of the basin below a waterfall or precipice. The line is restored as an indented continuation of Taqitçubo, not a new entry or page furniture.
